question: Using the SEBI Master Circulars for Investment Advisers and Research Analysts dated 6 February 2026, assess this plan for a partnership firm registered as both an IA and an RA. Its peak client counts in the previous financial year were 280 advisory clients and 425 research clients; it currently has only 120 clients in each business. For an ordinary, non-accredited individual client family, it proposes fixed annual fees of Rs 160,000 for investment advice and Rs 160,000 for research, excluding statutory charges. It wants to collect 18 months of fees upfront and retain three months of fees if either contract is terminated early. It also wants to operate advisory and research as one undifferentiated service. Explain: (1) the dual-registration compliance and segregation requirements; (2) the annual fee ceiling and maximum advance period for each service; (3) how refunds and breakage fees differ between IA and RA; (4) the deposit required for each registration, the lien beneficiary, which client counts determine the deposit, and the deadline for updating it; and (5) which fee rules change for corporate clients or accredited investors. Cite both circulars and distinguish their rules.

response.answer: For dual-registration compliance, an individual or partnership firm registered as an investment adviser or research analyst may hold both registrations, provided it complies with the rules, regulations, and reporting requirements under each set of regulations (IA Regulations and RA Regulations) separately [1][2]. Furthermore, the IA/RA must provide an undertaking stating that it will maintain an arms-length relationship between its activity as an IA and an RA, and ensure that its investment advisory services and research services are clearly segregated from each other [1][2]. The firm's proposal to operate advisory and research as one undifferentiated service is not permitted because the regulations explicitly require the two services to be clearly segregated [1][2]. Regarding annual fee ceilings and advance periods, for investment advisory services under the Master Circular for Investment Advisers, the fixed annual fee limit is Rs 1,51,000 per annum per family of client [3][4], and advance fees cannot exceed a period of one year [5][3]. For research services under the Master Circular for Research Analysts, the fee limit is also a maximum of Rs 1,51,000 per annum per family of client for individuals and HUF clients [6][7]. Regarding the advance period for research services, the excerpts contain an inconsistency: one passage states that advance fees shall not exceed the period stipulated by SEBI, presently one quarter [8], while another passage states that advance fees shall not exceed a period of one year [9]. The excerpts do not establish which provision takes precedence, so the inconsistency remains unresolved between the one-quarter limit [8] and the one-year limit [9]. For the proposed ordinary client, the proposed annual fee of Rs 160,000 for IA exceeds the cited limit of Rs 1,51,000 [3][4], and is therefore not permitted; similarly, the proposed annual fee of Rs 160,000 for RA exceeds the cited limit of Rs 1,51,000 [6][7], and is not permitted. Collecting 18 months of fees upfront exceeds both the IA one-year limit [5][3] and both RA advance period versions (one quarter [8] or one year [9]), and is therefore not permitted for either role. Regarding refunds and breakage fees upon early termination, for IA services, the client is entitled to a refund of proportionate fees for the unexpired period, and the IA is permitted to retain a maximum breakage fee not greater than one-quarter fee [5][10]. For RA services, the client is entitled to a refund of proportionate fees for the unexpired period, but the RA is explicitly prohibited from charging any breakage fee [9]. Therefore, the proposal to retain three months of fees as a breakage fee is permitted for IA (as it does not exceed one-quarter fee) [5][10], but is not permitted for RA because RAs cannot charge any breakage fee [9]. Regarding deposit requirements, the deposit for IA is maintained in the form of units of liquid mutual fund, an overnight mutual fund, or a deposit with a scheduled bank, and must be marked as a lien in favor of IAASB [11]. The deposit for RA is maintained in the same financial instruments and must be marked as a lien in favor of RAASB [12][13]. A lien is not a payment to the supervisory body. The deposit amounts are determined based on the maximum number of clients on any day of the previous financial year [11][13]. Using the historical maximum counts from the scenario (280 advisory clients and 425 research clients), the required deposit for IA is Rs 2 lakhs (for the 151 to 300 client bracket) [14][11], and the required deposit for RA is Rs 5 lakhs (for the 301 to 1,000 client bracket) [12][15]. The deadline for updating the deposit amount for any change in the applicable amount based on the previous year's maximum clients is latest by April 30th of the subsequent financial year [11][12]. Finally, regarding corporate clients (non-individual clients) and accredited investors, the fee-related provisions—including the fixed fee limit, modes of payment, refund rules, advance fee limits, and breakage fees—are not applicable; instead, fee-related terms and conditions for non-individual clients and accredited investors are governed through bilaterally negotiated contractual terms [14][9][3].
